Right Hand
RITE HAND
n. phrase
Plain English rendering Hebrew yamin and Greek dexia, both meaning the right side. In the ancient world the right hand was the hand of strength, of oath-taking, of blessing, and of the place of honor beside a king.

Biblical Definition

Right hand is one of Scripture's heaviest phrases, and it carries three loads. First, power: Thy right hand, O LORD, is become glorious in power: thy right hand, O LORD, hath dashed in pieces the enemy (Exod 15:6)—the LORD's right hand is His acting strength in history. Second, favor and joy: at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore (Ps 16:11), and the sheep are set on the right hand in the judgment. Third, and decisively, the enthronement of the Son. Psalm 110 opens with a line the New Testament quotes more than any other Old Testament verse: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool (Ps 110:1). Christ applies it to Himself before the Sanhedrin; Peter preaches it at Pentecost; Hebrews organizes its entire argument around it—the priest who sat down, because the work was finished. Mark records the ascension in the same terms: he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God (Mark 16:19). Stephen sees the one exception to the sitting: Jesus standing on the right hand of God (Acts 7:55), the enthroned Lord risen to His feet for a dying martyr. The right hand is therefore not a location in space but a statement of rank, authority and acceptance—which is why the Creed says it and why it matters that a man in our nature is there.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 notes that the right hand denotes the place of honor and of power—the side of dignity and strength—and that to be at one's right hand is to hold the position of favor and authority.

expand to see more

RIGHT HAND — The hand opposite to the left; among all nations, the hand of strength and of honor. To sit at the right hand of a prince is to occupy the place of highest dignity and authority.

In Scripture, the right hand of God denotes his power and his favor; and Christ's session at the right hand of the Father denotes his exaltation, dominion, and finished priestly work.

Key Scripture

Psalm 110:1 — "The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

Mark 16:19 — "So then after the Lord had spoken unto them, he was received up into heaven, and sat on the right hand of God."

Acts 7:55 — "But he, being full of the Holy Ghost, looked up stedfastly into heaven, and saw the glory of God, and Jesus standing on the right hand of God,"

Psalm 16:11 — "Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore."

Modern Corruption

Where the phrase survives at all it means a useful subordinate—someone's right-hand man—which loses both the enthronement it names in Scripture and the finished work signaled by the fact that the Priest sat down.

expand to see more

Modern usage keeps a shadow of the honor sense: a right-hand man is a trusted lieutenant. Scripture's meaning is enthronement, not assistance. Psalm 110:1 has a Lord seated beside the LORD, sharing the throne, with enemies being made a footstool in the interval—which is why the verse is the New Testament's favorite proof of Christ's deity and present reign. Reduced to a metaphor for a capable deputy, the phrase can no longer do that work.

The detail most often lost is the posture. Hebrews contrasts the priests who standeth daily ministering, whose work is never finished, with the one who after he had offered one sacrifice for sins for ever, sat down on the right hand of God. The sitting is the argument: no further offering is needed or possible. And Stephen's vision is the deliberate exception that proves it—the seated Lord standing for a servant being stoned. Both postures preach, and a reader who hears only right-hand man will catch neither.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yamin, the right hand or south side, the hand of strength and oath; Greek dexios, right—the side of honor at a throne.

expand to see more

Hebrew yamin (H3225) — the right hand or side; the hand of power, of blessing, and of the oath (Exod 15:6; Ps 16:11; 110:1; Isa 41:10).

Greek dexios (G1188) — right, of the right side; used of Christ's session, of the sheep in the judgment, and of the right hand of fellowship (Matt 25:33; Mark 16:19; Acts 7:55; Gal 2:9).

Greek kathizō (G2523) — to sit down, be seated; the verb whose perfect force carries the argument of Hebrews, the priest who sat (Heb 1:3; 8:1; 10:12; 12:2).

Usage

"Sit thou at my right hand—the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most."

"The Priest sat down; the work is finished. Levitical priests never sat."

"Stephen sees Him standing—the enthroned Lord on His feet for a dying martyr."
